title: pkix-path never applies dNSName name constraints to the CN; OpenSSL does
description:
pkix-path accepts chains OpenSSL rejects as name-constraint violations, because it never consults the subject commonName. Both CN references in pkix-path/src/lib.rs are inside #[cfg(test)] modules; production code looks only at dNSName SANs.

Demonstrated, not inferred. Three chains, root -> ICA (nameConstraints) -> EE, built with openssl and run through both oracles via 'pkix-difftest single':

  CN                 EE SANs      ICA constraint              openssl                      pkix-path
  bar.example.com    none         excluded DNS:bar.example.com  Fail: excluded subtree viol.  Pass
  John Smith         email only   permitted DNS:example.com     OK                            -
  notallowed.test    email only   permitted DNS:example.com     Fail: permitted subtree viol. Pass

So OpenSSL's rule is: when a certificate presents no dNSName SAN, apply dNSName constraints to the commonName if the CN is hostname-shaped, in both the permitted and excluded directions. A CN that is not hostname-shaped ('John Smith') is skipped, so the check does not reject certificates whose CN was never a hostname. pkix-path passes all three.

Reproduce with:
  openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout root.key -out root.pem -subj /CN=Root -addext basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE -addext keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign
  # ICA ext: basicConstraints=critical,CA:TRUE / keyUsage=critical,keyCertSign / nameConstraints=critical,excluded;DNS:bar.example.com
  # EE  ext: basicConstraints=critical,CA:FALSE / keyUsage=critical,digitalSignature  (and NO subjectAltName)
  # EE subject: /CN=bar.example.com
  openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted ica.pem ee.pem

Why it matters beyond the abstract. RFC 5280 does not require checking the CN, and reading a CN as a hostname is deprecated (RFC 6125 §6.4.4), which pkix-identity::verify_dns_name honours -- it returns MissingSan rather than falling back. But RFC 7672 §3.2.3 still REQUIRES CN fallback for SMTP DANE, and pkix-dane::verify_smtp_name does it via verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback. That path is reachable only under TlsaUsage::DaneTa -- DANE-EE(3) returns NotRequired per §3.2.1 and PKIX-TA/PKIX-EE are refused as PkixUsageUnusable -- and DANE-TA does validate a chain, so an intermediate's dNSName constraints are in play.

Composed: an intermediate forbidden from bar.example.com issues an EE with no SAN and CN=bar.example.com; pkix-path finds no dNSName SAN so the exclusion matches nothing and the path is valid; verify_smtp_name then matches the CN and reports Matched. The CA's exclusion is evaded.

Note this needs no wildcard. It was found while chasing a wildcard-CN variant of PKIX-bhtl, and the wildcard turned out to be irrelevant: a CN equal to the excluded name evades the constraint by itself. PKIX-bhtl's fix does not cover this, because that one bounded a wildcard SAN's coverage and this certificate has no SAN at all.

Recommended fix: mirror OpenSSL. In check_name_constraints, when the certificate presents no dNSName SAN, also check a hostname-shaped commonName against the dNSName subtrees in both directions.

The decision to make is the hostname-shaped test, because it is a heuristic in a security boundary and it is what bounds the false-rejection tail. OpenSSL's answer is observable above: it skipped 'John Smith' and checked 'notallowed.test'. A reasonable rule is at least one dot plus all labels being LDH (letters, digits, hyphen) with no spaces, which admits both demonstrated cases correctly. Too loose and a descriptive CN gets read as a hostname and rejected; too tight and an attacker picks a CN that evades the test but is still matched by verify_dns_name_with_cn_fallback, which has no such heuristic -- so the two tests must agree, the same coupling requirement PKIX-bhtl's fix had with pkix-identity's wildcard matcher.

Alternative considered and dispreferred: expose the accumulated constraints on ValidatedPath so the DANE layer can check a CN it actually matched. That has no false-rejection tail at all, since it only checks a name the certificate is genuinely asserting, but ValidatedPath exposes only anchor_index and depth today, so it needs new public API, and it leaves pkix-path accepting a chain OpenSSL rejects -- which is a divergence worth closing on its own, independent of DANE.

Also worth noting: INTEROP.md's 'Current status' says zero correctness regressions were detected against OpenSSL across the 247 classifiable PKITS chains. That remains true -- PKITS has no vector of this shape -- but this is a case where pkix-path is more lenient than OpenSSL, which is the opposite direction from every divergence currently documented there.
